title: Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required
description: This control is valid for AKS Automatic clusters, not only AKS Standard clusters. Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization is preconfigured in AKS Automatic, and cluster creation through the Azure CLI automatically assigns the creator the Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Cluster Admin role. Kubernetes RBAC remains relevant for service accounts and any Kubernetes RBAC bindings created in the cluster, so both authorization paths must be reviewed. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.1 Ensure that the cluster-admin role is only used where required

audit.command: This audit statement identifies the principals that are granted the Kubernetes cluster-admin role by reviewing ClusterRoleBinding assignments in the AKS cluster. It filters the binding output to show each binding name and the associated user, group, or service account, allowing the reviewer to determine which identities have unrestricted cluster administrative access.

remediation.command: Review all ClusterRoleBinding objects that grant access to the Kubernetes cluster-admin role and identify the users, groups, or service accounts associated with each binding. Validate whether each principal still requires full cluster administrative access or whether its responsibilities can be met through a lower privileged role, preferably a namespace Role/RoleBinding or a more limited ClusterRole, in accordance with AKS and Kubernetes least privilege guidance. Where full administrative access is not required, first assign the principal to an approved lower privilege role and confirm that required operational tasks continue to function as expected. After the replacement access has been validated, remove the unnecessary cluster-admin binding to reduce the risk of privilege escalation and cluster misuse. kubectl delete clusterrolebinding [name]

title: Minimize the admission of privileged containers
description: Minimize the admission of privileged containers by restricting the ability to create Pods whose containers, init containers, or ephemeral containers run with securityContext.privileged=true, and reserve that capability for narrowly approved platform scenarios only. AKS Automatic enables Deployment Safeguards and baseline Pod Security Standards in Enforce mode by default, providing built in admission controls for privileged workloads. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.1 Minimize the admission of privileged containers

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.ephemeralContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.privileged}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($4=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: AKS Automatic already enforces baseline Pod Security Standards and Deployment Safeguards. Remove privileged mode from user workloads rather than adding another admission policy. To enforce the restricted Pod Security Standard for a namespace, set the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label: kubectl label --overwrite ns NAMESPACE pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted The command enforces the restricted policy for the specified namespace. Where an exception is required, use an approved namespace exclusion and limit who can manage it. Deployment Safeguards are already enabled in Enforce mode. Use Azure Policy only when additional centralized policy requirements are needed.

title: Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required
description: Verify that access to Kubernetes Secret objects in AKS is granted only to identities with a defined purpose. The review should include Azure role assignments used by Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API, Kubernetes RBAC roles and bindings, and service account permissions, with particular attention to permissions that allow get, list, or watch access to secrets, because those permissions expose sensitive namespace data. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.2 Ensure access to Secrets is minimized and granted only where required

audit.command: Review the users, groups, and service accounts that have get, list, or watch access to Secret objects in the Kubernetes API. Identify these permissions in Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole rules, then trace the associated RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects to the affected identities. Because Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API is preconfigured in AKS Automatic, also review Azure role assignments to users, groups, service principals, and managed identities that allow access to Secrets.

remediation.command: Where access is not required, remove get, list, and watch access to Secret objects in the cluster. For Kubernetes RBAC, remove the unnecessary verbs from the applicable Role or ClusterRole, or remove the binding that grants the role to the identity. For Microsoft Entra ID authorization, replace broad assignments with a role that does not permit Secret access, such as Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader when read access to other resources is sufficient. Confirm that workloads, controllers, and administrative processes continue to function with the replacement permissions before removing the existing access.

title: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used
description: Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used by verifying that application and automation pods in AKS Automatic do not rely on the namespace default service account when a dedicated service account should be used instead. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Fails when a default service account does not set automountServiceAccountToken: false or is bound to a Role/ClusterRole.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.5 Ensure that default service accounts are not actively used

audit.command:
sa=$(kubectl get serviceaccounts -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{if eq .metadata.name "default"}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.automountServiceAccountToken}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
rb=$(kubectl get rolebindings,clusterrolebindings -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$b:=.metadata.name}}{{$bn:=.metadata.namespace}}{{range .subjects}}{{if eq .kind "ServiceAccount"}}{{if eq .name "default"}}{{if .namespace}}{{.namespace}}{{else}}{{$bn}}{{end}} {{$b}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$sa" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && $2!="false" {print "automount: " $1}')
bad2=$(printf '%s
' "$rb" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex {print "binding: " $0}')
if [ -z "$bad$bad2" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
%s
' "$bad" "$bad2" | grep . | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Apply the following steps to replace default service account usage with dedicated workload identities in AKS Automatic: • Update workloads to explicitly set a dedicated serviceAccountName instead of inheriting the namespace default service account. • Remove unnecessary RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding assignments from the default service account, and keep any remaining access minimal and limited to the required namespace. • Set automountServiceAccountToken to false where Kubernetes API access is not required to prevent automatic token mounting. • Review both the ServiceAccount and Pod settings for automountServiceAccountToken, and treat the Pod value as authoritative when both are defined. • For workloads that need Azure resource access, use Microsoft Entra Workload ID with a dedicated service account and explicit workload configuration instead of the namespace default service account.

title: Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary
description: Verify that service account tokens in AKS Automatic are mounted only for pods that require Kubernetes API access or an explicitly configured workload identity flow. Confirm that pods and service accounts are not broadly relying on default token mounting, and that token projection is limited to workloads with a defined operational need. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports pods with an auto-mounted service account token (kube-api-access-* volume).
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.6 Ensure that Service Account Tokens are only mounted where necessary

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.volumes}} {{.name}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($0 ~ / kube-api-access-/)')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Apply the following steps to reduce unnecessary service account token mounting in AKS Automatic: • Set automountServiceAccountToken to false for pods and service accounts that do not require Kubernetes API access. • Update workloads to use a dedicated serviceAccountName only where a service account token is operationally required, instead of inheriting token behavior from the namespace default service account. • For workloads that need Azure resource access, use the preconfigured Microsoft Entra Workload ID with a dedicated service account, the required pod label, and explicit workload configuration rather than broad default token mounting. • Revalidate workloads after the change to confirm that only pods with a documented need continue to receive service account tokens.

title: Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster
description: Roles and ClusterRoles that grant bind, impersonate, or escalate should be assigned only when strictly required. These permissions can bypass normal RBAC safeguards and allow a principal to acquire or grant authority beyond its current permissions. Review AKS Automatic authorization assignments to ensure bind, escalate, and impersonate permissions are granted only to identities with a documented administrative need. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.7 Limit use of the Bind, Impersonate and Escalate permissions in the Kubernetes cluster

audit.command: Review AKS Automatic RBAC to identify any users, groups, or service accounts granted bind, escalate, or impersonate permissions through Kubernetes RBAC or Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API. • Identify Roles and ClusterRoles that include bind, escalate, or impersonate, then trace the RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings that assign them. • Determine which users, groups, or service accounts receive those permissions. • Validate that each assignment is required for a defined administrative function.

remediation.command: Remove bind, escalate, and impersonate permissions from any custom Role, ClusterRole, or Azure custom role that does not require them for an approved administrative function. Where these permissions are required, keep them limited to the required resources and namespace and avoid assigning them to workload service accounts. • Update each affected custom Role to remove unnecessary bind, escalate, or impersonate rules. • Update each affected custom ClusterRole to retain only the specific elevated permission that is explicitly required. • Remove unnecessary corresponding DataActions from Azure custom roles used to authorize access to the Kubernetes API. • Replace broad assignments with roles that have fewer permissions, and limit access to the required namespace rather than the entire cluster where possible.

title: Minimize access to webhook configuration objects
description: Minimize access to webhook configuration objects so that only tightly controlled cluster administrative identities can create, update, or delete ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration resources in AKS. Admission controllers run after authentication and authorization but before an object is persisted, and Microsoft’s AKS documentation shows that webhook configurations define the webhook service endpoint and related trust ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.11 Minimize access to webhook configuration objects

audit.command: Audit this control by identifying who can modify cluster webhook configuration resources and confirming that webhook definitions are limited to approved admission use cases in AKS. Verify that ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects are present only where operationally required, that their coverage is not broader than necessary, and that access to manage them is restricted through least privilege RBAC. Misconfigured admission webhooks can disrupt cluster operations, especially when they apply too broadly or affect AKS managed resources.

remediation.command: Remove permission to create, update, patch, or delete ValidatingWebhookConfiguration and MutatingWebhookConfiguration objects from broad ClusterRole assignments, then bind that access only to tightly controlled cluster administrative identities. Use least privilege Kubernetes RBAC and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, which is preconfigured in AKS Automatic, with access granted through centrally managed identity groups rather than widely distributed individual assignments. Review service account permissions so workload identities do not inherit cluster webhook management capability. Remove unnecessary Azure role assignments or webhook configuration permissions from custom roles. Review each webhook configuration and narrow its match criteria to only the required namespaces, resources, and operations.

title: Minimize access to the service account token creation
description: Minimize access to service account token creation so that only tightly controlled administrative or platform identities can request tokens for Kubernetes service accounts in AKS. AKS uses service accounts as a core Kubernetes identity type and documents that workloads can use Service Account Token Volume Projection to obtain a Kubernetes token. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.12 Minimize access to the service account token creation

audit.command: Confirm that the ability to create service account tokens is limited to identities that require it for approved platform or workload operations. Service accounts remain Kubernetes identities governed by Kubernetes RBAC. AKS Automatic preconfigures Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, so review its Azure role assignments alongside Kubernetes RBAC bindings. • Review both Kubernetes RBAC and the preconfigured Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. • Review Role and ClusterRole rules for create access to serviceaccounts/token, including wildcard verbs or resources.

remediation.command: Review all Role and ClusterRole definitions for access to the serviceaccounts/token subresource. Remove that permission from any user, group, CI/CD identity, or workload service account that does not have a documented operational requirement. Also review the preconfigured Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization because Microsoft Entra identities and Kubernetes service accounts follow different authorization paths. 1. Review Role and ClusterRole objects for serviceaccounts/token access. 2. Remove that permission from broad operational roles, CI/CD identities, and workload service accounts. 3. Reassign it only to approved administrative or platform identities with a documented need. 4. Remove unnecessary Azure role assignments or custom role permissions that provide equivalent access. 5. Validate that required workload identity and projected token flows still function correctly. 6.

title: Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host process ID namespace
description: Minimize the admission of Pods that request spec.hostPID=true so that only tightly controlled, explicitly approved platform workloads can share the host process ID namespace in AKS. Users, groups, and service accounts with deployment rights should not be able to create or update workloads that use host PID sharing without an approved exception. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.2 Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host process ID namespace

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{.metadata.namespace}} {{.metadata.name}} {{.spec.hostPID}}{{"
"}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($3=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: AKS Automatic already enforces baseline Pod Security Standards and Deployment Safeguards. Remove spec.hostPID: true from user workloads that do not have an approved exception. Where an exception is required, use an approved namespace exclusion and limit who can manage it. Deployment Safeguards are already enabled in Enforce mode. Use Azure Policy only when additional centralized policy requirements are needed. Validate required workloads after making changes.

AKS Automatic enables Deployment Safeguards and baseline Pod Security Standards in Enforce mode by default. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.3 Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host IPC namespace

Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.4 Minimize the admission of containers wishing to share the host network namespace

title: Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation
description: Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation=true so that users, groups, and service accounts with deployment rights cannot broadly create Pods containing regular, init, or ephemeral containers that permit a process to gain more privileges than its parent. Microsoft documents allowPrivilegeEscalation as a container security context setting that should be designed to stay false. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation: true are reported.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.5 Minimize the admission of containers with allowPrivilegeEscalation

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{range .spec.ephemeralContainers}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{.name}} {{with .securityContext}}{{.allowPrivilegeEscalation}}{{end}}{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && ($4=="true")')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Add policies to each namespace in the cluster which has user workloads to restrict the admission of containers with securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation set to true or left unset. Use the restricted Pod Security Standard or an equivalent Azure Policy control because the preconfigured baseline policy does not enforce this field.

title: Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for AKS workloads
description: It is important to use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts in AKS so identity, permissions, and token use are isolated to the specific workload that requires them, rather than shared across unrelated pods. Kubernetes service accounts remain a core Kubernetes identity construct and also serve as the anchor for Microsoft Entra Workload ID, which allows access to Kubernetes and Azure resources to be assigned per workload. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.2.1 Use dedicated Kubernetes service accounts for AKS workloads

audit.command: For each namespace, verify that workloads do not use the default service account unless required, and confirm that the default service account has no custom role bindings beyond baseline defaults. Review service accounts used by individual workloads to ensure permissions follow least privilege, and confirm automountServiceAccountToken is disabled where token access is not needed. • Review each namespace for pods and workload controllers that use the default service account, and flag any use that is not explicitly required.

remediation.command: Use a dedicated Kubernetes service account for each AKS workload that requires identity, and replace use of the namespace default service account wherever it is not explicitly required. Limit each service account to only the Kubernetes permissions and Azure resource access needed by that workload, and prevent service account tokens from being mounted into pods unless token access is required. 1. Create a separate Kubernetes service account for each workload or application boundary that requires distinct access. 2. Bind each service account only to the minimum required Kubernetes Role or ClusterRole, and avoid granting custom permissions to the namespace default service account. Prefer a RoleBinding in the required namespace when permissions do not need to apply throughout the cluster. 3. Set automountServiceAccountToken: false for pods that do not need a service account token. 4.

title: Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets at rest with AKS KMS protection
description: Kubernetes Secret data stored by AKS in etcd must be protected with encryption at rest. When additional KMS protection is required, use the AKS KMS provider integrated with Azure Key Vault. Azure platform encryption provides baseline storage layer protection, while AKS KMS adds envelope encryption before Secret data is committed to etcd. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.3.1 Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets at rest with AKS KMS protection

audit.command: Review each AKS Automatic cluster to determine whether KMS encryption for Kubernetes Secrets is enabled and correctly configured. Azure platform encryption is always enabled for data at rest, but AKS KMS adds a separate encryption layer before Secret data is written to etcd. Verify that securityProfile.kubernetesResourceObjectEncryptionProfile.infras tructureEncryption is set to Enabled for the current KMS data encryption experience.

remediation.command: Enable AKS KMS on AKS Automatic clusters that require additional Kubernetes Secret encryption. Confirm that the selected KMS experience is supported for the cluster and that Preview use is approved where applicable. 1. Identify clusters where AKS KMS is not enabled. 2. Decide whether to use platform managed keys or customer managed keys based on key ownership and compliance requirements. 3. For customer managed keys, create or select the Azure Key Vault key, assign a user assigned managed identity, and grant the required key permissions before enabling KMS. 4. For a private Key Vault, configure the firewall to allow trusted Azure services and confirm that the managed identity can access the vault. 5. Verify that the AKS security profile shows infrastructure encryption enabled and, for customer managed keys, the expected Key Vault configuration. 6.

title: Use private AKS clusters and disable the public API server FQDN
description: Provisioning AKS in private cluster mode limits control plane exposure by placing the Kubernetes API server on private addressing and requiring connectivity through approved private network paths rather than broad public network access. AKS Automatic preconfigures API Server VNet Integration, which places the API server behind an internal load balancer address in a delegated subnet. Requires the az CLI (logged in) with read access to the cluster named by AKS_RG and AKS_NAME. Requires enablePrivateCluster true and enablePublicFqdn false.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.2 Use private AKS clusters and disable the public API server FQDN

audit.command:
out=$(az aks show --resource-group "${AKS_RG:?set AKS_RG}" --name "${AKS_NAME:?set AKS_NAME}" --query '[apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster, apiServerAccessProfile.enablePublicFqdn]' -o tsv) || exit 1
set -- $(printf '%s\n' "$out" | tr 'A-Z' 'a-z')
if [ "${1:-}" = true ] && [ "${2:-}" = false ]; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: enablePrivateCluster=${1:-} enablePublicFqdn=${2:-}"; fi

remediation.command: Use the apiServerAccessProfile results to determine whether the cluster must be moved to private cluster mode and whether the public FQDN must be disabled. Remediation should bring the cluster to enablePrivateCluster: true and, where required by policy, enablePublicFqdn: false; the detailed action depends on whether the cluster is new or existing. API Server VNet Integration is already preconfigured for AKS Automatic. 1. If enablePrivateCluster is false on a new deployment, create the cluster as private by using az aks create --sku automatic --enable-private-cluster --disable-public-fqdn when the requirement is to prevent publication of a public DNS name for the API server. 2. If enablePrivateCluster is false on an existing AKS Automatic cluster, enable private cluster mode through the supported AKS update path. A separate API Server VNet Integration conversion is not required. 3.

title: Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes
description: Node pools should use private IP addressing only and should not assign instance level public IPs to individual nodes unless a specific workload requires that design. Keeping nodes private reduces direct internet reachability of the worker node plane and helps ensure node access occurs through approved internal network paths, load balanced services, or controlled management methods rather than through per node public exposure. Requires the az CLI (logged in) with read access to the cluster named by AKS_RG and AKS_NAME. Fails when any node pool has enableNodePublicIP true.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.3 Ensure clusters are created with Private Nodes

audit.command:
out=$(az aks nodepool list --resource-group "${AKS_RG:?set AKS_RG}" --cluster-name "${AKS_NAME:?set AKS_NAME}" -o json) || exit 1
if printf '%s' "$out" | grep -Eiq '"enableNodePublicIp"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*true'; then echo noncompliant; else echo compliant; fi

remediation.command: Where AKS node pools are configured with node public IPs, the preferred remediation is to return them to the standard AKS networking model unless there is a clear workload requirement for direct per node public reachability. Node public IPs are an optional feature rather than the normal operating model, so remediation should focus on removing unnecessary node level internet exposure and shifting any needed inbound or outbound connectivity to supported service and egress patterns. AKS Automatic manages its system node pools, so those nodes and their underlying resources should not be modified directly. 1. Identify each node pool where enableNodePublicIP is enabled and confirm whether the setting is actually required for the workload, since AKS documents node public IPs as a special case feature. 2.

title: Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles
description: Verify that Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole definitions in AKS do not use wildcard entries such as * for verbs, resources, or apiGroups unless a documented administrative need exists. This is particularly relevant for service accounts because their authorization continues to rely on Kubernetes RBAC. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.3 Minimize wildcard use in Roles and ClusterRoles

audit.command: Review Kubernetes Role and ClusterRole definitions in the AKS cluster for wildcard use in verbs, resources, or apiGroups, and identify any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding that assigns those roles to users, groups, or service accounts. Retrieve the roles defined across all namespaces in the cluster and review for wildcards. kubectl get roles --all-namespaces -o yaml Retrieve the cluster roles defined in the cluster and review for wildcards kubectl get clusterroles -o yaml

remediation.command: Replace wildcard entries in Role and ClusterRole objects with only the specific verbs, resources, and apiGroups required for the workload or administrator function. Prefer Role and RoleBinding objects within the required namespace instead of permissions throughout the cluster wherever possible. This is particularly important for service accounts and controllers because wildcard Kubernetes RBAC rules can still grant excessive permissions to workloads even when human user access is managed through Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API.

title: Minimize access to create pods
description: The ability to create pods in a namespace can provide opportunities for privilege escalation, such as assigning privileged service accounts to these pods or mounting hostPath volumes with access to sensitive data. Pod Security Policies are no longer supported. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.4 Minimize access to create pods

audit.command: Review Azure role assignments used by Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API and Kubernetes RBAC permissions granted to service accounts. Identify the users, groups, and service accounts that can create Pods. Confirm that each assignment is required for the principal’s function, with particular attention to service accounts and namespace write access. Flag unnecessary pod creation rights for remediation.

remediation.command: The following steps help reduce pod creation access to the minimum required in AKS Automatic: • Identify all Azure role assignments used by Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API and Kubernetes RBAC bindings that allow pod creation, including access within a namespace and access throughout the cluster. • Remove pod creation rights from any user, group, or service account that does not have a documented operational need. • Replace broad permissions with a role that has only the required permissions, preferably limited to the required namespace rather than throughout the cluster. • Ensure workloads use dedicated service accounts with only the permissions required for the application or controller. • Revalidate access after changes to confirm required workloads still run and unnecessary pod creation rights have been removed.

title: Minimize access to create persistent storage
description: Permission to create persistent storage in AKS Automatic is granted only where it is required. This includes direct creation of PersistentVolume objects and, more commonly, creation of PersistentVolumeClaim objects that reference an existing StorageClass and cause a CSI driver to provision an Azure Disk, Azure Files share, or other supported storage resource. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.8 Minimize access to create persistent storage

audit.command: Review AKS Automatic authorization to identify any users, groups, or service accounts that can create PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim, or StorageClass resources. Review the applicable Kubernetes Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, and ClusterRoleBinding objects. Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API is preconfigured in AKS Automatic, so also review direct and inherited Azure role assignments and custom roles that grant these permissions.

remediation.command: Remove persistent storage creation rights from any user, group, or service account that does not require them. Replace unnecessary Azure role assignments or Kubernetes RBAC bindings with roles that provide only the required permissions. Limit direct PersistentVolume and StorageClass administration to approved administrators, and allow workloads to create PersistentVolumeClaim objects only in the required namespace. Kubernetes RBAC does not restrict which existing StorageClass a principal can name in a claim. If workloads must be limited to approved storage classes, enforce that requirement through an admission policy, such as Azure Policy for Kubernetes, which is enabled on AKS Automatic. After making changes, verify that required applications can still provision storage through the intended AKS CSI driver path.

title: Minimize access to the nodes/proxy subresource
description: Review AKS authorization to ensure access to the nodes/proxy subresource is granted only to identities with a documented operational need. Review Kubernetes ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects, service accounts that receive this access, and applicable Azure role assignments because Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization is preconfigured in AKS Automatic. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.9 Minimize access to the nodes/proxy subresource

audit.command: Review custom Kubernetes ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding objects that grant access to the nodes/proxysubresource. Include rules that grant nodes/proxy directly or through resource wildcards such asnodes/or`. Confirm that each assignment is required for an approved troubleshooting, maintenance, or platform administration function. Also review direct and inherited Azure role assignments and custom roles that permit this resource or all Kubernetes resources because Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization is preconfigured in AKS Automatic.

remediation.command: Reduce custom RBAC access to the nodes/proxy API path so it is limited to approved administrative identities that require kubelet access. • Remove nodes/proxy, nodes/*, or applicable wildcard rules from any custom ClusterRole that does not require kubelet proxy access. • Where node data is still required, use the narrower node subresource and verbs supported by the current AKS release instead of nodes/proxy. • Remove any ClusterRoleBinding that grants this access to a workload service account, CI/CD identity, or operator group without an approved requirement. • Remove equivalent Azure role assignments or custom role permissions that are not required. Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization is preconfigured in AKS Automatic.

title: Minimize access to the approval subresource of CertificateSigningRequests objects
description: Minimize access to the approval subresource of CertificateSigningRequests objects so that only tightly controlled administrative identities can approve certificate requests in AKS. AKS uses certificates for component authentication. Kubelets use CSRs as part of client certificate bootstrap and rotation. AKS authorization is intentionally granular and is meant to give users, groups, and service accounts access only to the resources they require. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.1.10 Minimize access to the approval subresource of CertificateSigningRequests objects

audit.command: Audit this control by reviewing how privileged access is granted across the AKS authorization model and verifying that CSR approval authority is limited to approved administrative identities. This is not a discrete platform setting. It is a least privilege review across Microsoft Entra integration, Kubernetes RBAC, and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization, which is preconfigured in AKS Automatic.

remediation.command: Remove certificatesigningrequests/approval access from any ClusterRole that is not explicitly required for cluster certificate administration, then bind that capability only to approved AKS administrative identities. Use Microsoft Entra integration with least privilege Kubernetes RBAC and the preconfigured Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization while limiting cluster permissions to approved identities. Remove unnecessary Azure role assignments or CSR write permissions from custom roles. Validate that expected AKS certificate workflows, such as kubelet TLS bootstrapping and rotation, continue to generate approved CSRs after permissions are tightened. Do not modify AKS managed system roles or bindings.

title: Prefer exposing secrets as mounted files rather than environment variables
description: Prefer exposing secrets to AKS workloads as mounted files rather than as environment variables, particularly when secrets are sourced from Azure Key Vault through the Secrets Store CSI Driver. In current AKS guidance, the Key Vault integration model is volume based, with secrets made available at a mounted path inside the container, and Microsoft documents that mounted content can be synchronized and rotated through the CSI provider. Requires kubectl with cluster-wide read access (KUBECONFIG); system namespaces are excluded and listed resources must be remediated or documented as exceptions. Reports containers using env valueFrom.secretKeyRef or envFrom.secretRef.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.4.1 Prefer exposing secrets as mounted files rather than environment variables

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods -A -o go-template='{{range .items}}{{$ns:=.metadata.namespace}}{{$p:=.metadata.name}}{{range .spec.containers}}{{$c:=.name}}{{range .env}}{{if .valueFrom}}{{if .valueFrom.secretKeyRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} env{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{range .envFrom}}{{if .secretRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} envFrom{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{range .spec.initContainers}}{{$c:=.name}}{{range .env}}{{if .valueFrom}}{{if .valueFrom.secretKeyRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} env{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{range .envFrom}}{{if .secretRef}}{{$ns}} {{$p}} {{$c}} envFrom{{"
"}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}{{end}}') || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s
' "$out" | awk -v ex='^(kube-system|kube-public|kube-node-lease|gatekeeper-system|azure-arc)$' 'NF && $1 !~ ex && (1)')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s
' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Move workloads away from secret backed environment variables and toward file based secret delivery through mounted volumes, preferably using the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver. Mounted secrets support sync and autorotation, while secrets exposed through environment variables do not update in running pods until those pods are restarted. 1. Identify workloads that use secretKeyRef or envFrom.secretRef and classify them for migration. 2. Replace environment variable injection with mounted secret files, ideally through SecretProviderClass and the Secrets Store CSI Driver using the Workload Identity capability preconfigured by AKS Automatic. 3. Enable secret autorotation where supported so mounted content and synced Kubernetes Secrets are refreshed automatically. 4.

title: Consider external secret storage
description: Consider external secret storage for AKS workloads by storing sensitive values in Azure Key Vault and retrieving them at runtime through the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver instead of treating Kubernetes Secret objects in the cluster as the primary secret system. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.4.2 Consider external secret storage

audit.command: Audit secrets management by confirming that sensitive values are stored externally, delivered to pods through the AKS supported secret path, and rotated without relying on manual redeployments. Microsoft’s current AKS guidance centers on Azure Key Vault, the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver, and mounted secret delivery with autorotation support. • Verify secrets are primarily stored in Azure Key Vault, not embedded in code, manifests, or pipelines.

remediation.command: Move sensitive application secrets that are appropriate for external storage out of Kubernetes native storage and deployment artifacts and into Azure Key Vault. Deliver those secrets to pods at runtime through the Azure Key Vault provider for Secrets Store CSI Driver. Pair the CSI driver with Microsoft Entra Workload ID using the Workload Identity and OIDC issuer capabilities preconfigured by AKS Automatic. The add on managed identity may be used when appropriate. Use mounted secret files as the primary consumption path and enable autorotation where secret freshness matters. Retain Kubernetes Secret objects only where required for Kubernetes functions or an approved synchronization pattern. • Inventory secrets currently stored in code, manifests, pipelines, or standalone Kubernetes Secret objects and identify sensitive application secrets appropriate for migration to Key Vault.

title: Ensure container image vulnerability scanning with Defender for Containers or a third-party provider
description: Ensure vulnerability scanning is enabled for container images that are stored in registries and intended for deployment to AKS, using Microsoft Defender for Containers, Defender CSPM where supported, or an equivalent third party scanner. This control applies both to registry images and, where enabled and supported, to running containers in AKS. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.1 Ensure container image vulnerability scanning with Defender for Containers or a third-party provider

audit.command: Review whether Microsoft Defender for Containers or Defender CSPM is enabled for the subscription and whether registry image vulnerability assessment is enabled under that plan. For AKS, also verify the cluster Defender profile when cluster side monitoring is in scope, and confirm Defender for Cloud is generating vulnerability findings for relevant images. For an AKS Automatic cluster using a Helm based Defender sensor, verify the Helm release in the kube-system namespace instead of relying only on the AKS Defender profile.

remediation.command: Enable Microsoft Defender for Containers for the subscription, enable the registry vulnerability assessment capability used for container image scanning, and then verify that Defender for Cloud is producing vulnerability findings for the registries and AKS workloads in scope. If the control is intended to cover only registry image scanning, the subscription plan and Registry access settings are the key fixes. If it also includes AKS runtime protection, deploy the Defender sensor or AKS built in integration and confirm the cluster Defender profile is enabled. 1. In the Defender for Cloud Environment settings, turn Containers from Free to Standard. 2. Enable the registry image assessment capability by turning on the registry related extension, including ContainerRegistriesVulnerabilityAssessments and required Registry access for supported registries. 3.

title: Minimize and scope access to Azure Container Registry (ACR)
description: Limit ACR access for AKS Automatic and related users to only the permissions required for their function. AKS to ACR integration grants the cluster’s kubelet managed identity the AcrPull role so nodes can pull images without broader registry rights. For ABAC enabled registries, --attach-acr is not supported, and the Container Registry Repository Reader role must be assigned manually instead. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.2 Minimize and scope access to Azure Container Registry (ACR)

audit.command: Review ACR access for AKS Automatic to confirm the registry uses least privilege, identity based access. Verify the ACR admin account is disabled, determine whether the registry is using RBAC only or RBAC + ABAC, confirm the AKS kubelet identity has only image pull rights, and review other principals for unnecessary push, delete, or broader registry permissions. • Confirm that adminUserEnabled is false, since the local admin account provides broad registry access and is not the preferred authentication method for integrated AKS and ACR use.

remediation.command: Disable the ACR local admin account and use identity based, least privilege access for registry authentication and authorization. For AKS Automatic, use the kubelet managed identity for required image pull access, and assign only the minimum registry role required by the registry authorization model: AcrPull for registries using RBAC only or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC enabled registries. Do not use --attach-acr with an ABAC enabled registry. Assign Container Registry Repository Reader manually to the kubelet managed identity and add repository conditions where required. Human users should use Microsoft Entra identities, while pipelines and workloads should use managed identities or service principals with only the required registry roles and repository conditions, rather than shared local registry credentials.

title: Limit AKS access to pull images from Azure Container Registry (ACR)
description: Configure AKS Automatic with pull only access to ACR so the cluster can pull the images it needs to run workloads without being able to modify registry content. This is implemented by granting the kubelet managed identity only the required pull permission, typically AcrPull for registries using RBAC only, or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC enabled registries, so cluster access is limited to image retrieval rather than push, delete, ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.3 Limit AKS access to pull images from Azure Container Registry (ACR)

audit.command: Review AKS Automatic access to ACR to confirm the cluster is limited to image pull access and does not have broader registry permissions. Identify the registry authorization mode, confirm the kubelet managed identity is used for ACR access, and verify that the cluster has only the minimum read role required for image pulls. • Determine whether the registry uses RBAC Registry Permissions or RBAC Registry + ABAC Repository Permissions, because this affects the expected pull role and access model.

remediation.command: Restrict AKS Automatic access to ACR so the cluster can only pull images needed for workload startup and cannot push, delete, or administer registry content. Use the kubelet managed identity for registry authentication and assign only the minimum pull role required by the registry authorization mode: AcrPull for registries using RBAC only or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC enabled registries. Do not use --attach-acr with an ABAC enabled registry. Assign Container Registry Repository Reader manually to the kubelet managed identity. 1. Configure AKS Automatic to use the kubelet managed identity for ACR access rather than shared registry credentials. 2. Assign only the required pull role to the kubelet identity: AcrPull for registries using RBAC only, or Container Registry Repository Reader for ABAC enabled registries. 3.

title: Restrict AKS workloads to approved container registries only
description: Configure AKS Automatic so workloads pull images only from registries that have been explicitly approved by the organization, such as selected ACR instances or other trusted registries. This is typically enforced with Azure Policy by auditing or denying deployments whose image references do not match approved image source patterns, while AKS to ACR integration provides the managed identity and pull role pattern needed for authorized image ... The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.1.4 Restrict AKS workloads to approved container registries only

audit.command: Review AKS Automatic image source controls to confirm workloads are limited to approved container registries. The audit should verify that an Azure Policy definition or initiative is assigned to the cluster to audit or deny unapproved image sources, that the approved image source patterns are explicitly defined, and that AKS Automatic has valid pull access only to those approved registries. The presence of Azure Policy and Deployment Safeguards alone does not confirm that the allowed images policy or the organization’s approved patterns are configured.

remediation.command: Restrict AKS Automatic workloads to approved container registries by enforcing an Azure Policy control for allowed images or trusted registries, defining the approved image source patterns, and ensuring workloads reference only those registries. Use the Azure Policy add on with the built in allowed images policy, and deploy only validated images from approved sources. 1. Confirm that Azure Policy remains enabled on the AKS Automatic cluster. Assign the allowed images policy separately because the preconfigured safeguards do not define the organization’s approved registry patterns. 2. Assign an AKS policy or initiative that audits or denies unapproved image sources, and set the parameters to the organization’s approved image reference patterns. 3. Migrate or mirror workload images from external or nonapproved registries into an approved registry, such as ACR, before deployment.

title: Restrict Access to the Control Plane Endpoint
description: The AKS control plane endpoint should be exposed only through approved network paths rather than being broadly reachable. For AKS, the control plane is the Kubernetes API server. For public clusters, API server authorized IP ranges can be used to limit access to specific public IP addresses or CIDR blocks and deny all other sources. Requires the az CLI (logged in) with read access to the cluster named by AKS_RG and AKS_NAME. Passes for a private cluster or a public API server limited by authorized IP ranges (not 0.0.0.0/0).
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.1 Restrict Access to the Control Plane Endpoint

audit.command:
priv=$(az aks show --resource-group "${AKS_RG:?set AKS_RG}" --name "${AKS_NAME:?set AKS_NAME}" --query apiServerAccessProfile.enablePrivateCluster -o tsv) || exit 1
ranges=$(az aks show --resource-group "${AKS_RG:?set AKS_RG}" --name "${AKS_NAME:?set AKS_NAME}" --query 'apiServerAccessProfile.authorizedIpRanges' -o tsv) || exit 1
case "$priv" in [Tt]rue) echo compliant; exit 0;; esac
if [ -n "$ranges" ] && ! printf '%s\n' "$ranges" | grep -q '0\.0\.0\.0/0'; then echo compliant; else echo "noncompliant: public API server without authorized IP ranges"; fi

remediation.command: If the cluster is intended to expose the Kubernetes API server only over private network paths, use a private AKS cluster; if the cluster is already private but a public DNS name is still published, disable the public FQDN when required by the security standard. If the cluster must keep a public API server endpoint, configure authorized IP ranges so only approved administrator and egress CIDR ranges can reach it. Microsoft notes that authorized IP ranges apply only to the public API server endpoint, recommends including both the cluster egress IP and the networks used to administer the cluster, and states that rule updates can take up to two minutes to propagate. 1. If enablePrivateCluster is false and the cluster should be managed only over private connectivity, enable private cluster mode.

title: Use HTTPS with valid TLS certificates for externally exposed workloads
description: Protect externally exposed AKS applications by ensuring client connections use HTTPS with a valid TLS certificate instead of plaintext HTTP at the cluster entry point. That protection is typically applied at the ingress or gateway layer, where external web traffic is accepted and routed to backend services. Using TLS at that layer reduces the risk of exposing application traffic, credentials, session data, or other sensitive content in transit. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.4.4 Use HTTPS with valid TLS certificates for externally exposed workloads

audit.command: It is important to review this at the Ingress or Gateway layer, and at any public LoadBalancer Service that exposes web traffic directly, since those components are the primary enforcement points for external HTTP and TLS termination. The purpose of the review is to confirm that public application entry points are not exposing client traffic over plaintext HTTP and that every externally published hostname is protected by a certificate based HTTPS or TLS listener.

remediation.command: Remediate by ensuring every externally exposed AKS web entry point is published through an Ingress or Gateway listener configured for HTTPS/TLS, with a valid certificate bound to the public hostname. If a public LoadBalancer Service exposes a web application directly, configure TLS in the application or place the service behind an approved TLS terminating entry point. HTTPS protection is typically implemented at the Layer 7 ingress or gateway layer, where client traffic is accepted and TLS is terminated before traffic is forwarded to backend services. The remediation objective is to eliminate plaintext HTTP exposure for public application endpoints and standardize certificate based TLS for all external web traffic. Use the managed Application Routing Gateway API path provided by AKS Automatic unless the approved architecture requires another supported ingress implementation. 1.

title: Use Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API
description: Use Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 5.5.1 Use Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API

audit.command: Review the AKS cluster to confirm AKS managed Microsoft Entra integration is enabled and Microsoft Entra ID authorization for the Kubernetes API is turned on as expected for AKS Automatic. Then verify that access for users, groups, and service principals is being granted through Azure role assignments for Kubernetes authorization rather than primarily through Kubernetes RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects for those Entra identities.

remediation.command: AKS Automatic already provides Microsoft Entra integration and Azure RBAC for Kubernetes authorization, so remediation normally consists of correcting Azure role assignments rather than enabling the authorization model. For stronger control, pair this with disabling local accounts so static --admin access does not remain available as an alternate path. If local accounts are disabled on an existing cluster, rotate cluster certificates to revoke previously issued local account credentials. For custom resource access, use an approved custom role and Azure ABAC conditions to limit access to the required CRD groups and kinds where supported. 1. Confirm the preconfigured Microsoft Entra integration and Azure RBAC authorization settings remain enabled. Investigate any cluster that does not report the expected AKS Automatic values. 2.

title: Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces
description: Create administrative boundaries between resources by organizing AKS workloads into separate namespaces and scoping access to those namespaces with Kubernetes RBAC or Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization. Azure RBAC for Kubernetes Authorization is preconfigured in AKS Automatic, while Kubernetes RBAC remains applicable to service accounts and any additional Kubernetes RBAC bindings. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.5.1 Create administrative boundaries between resources using namespaces

audit.command: Verify that namespaces are not only present, but are being used as intentional administrative boundaries for teams, applications, or environments within the AKS cluster. Namespaces are the logical isolation boundary for workloads and resources in a shared cluster, and they should be paired with access controls and other governance within each namespace such as quotas and network policies. Namespaces alone are not sufficient for hostile multitenancy, so the audit should focus on whether they are being used consistently to separate administration and operations as intended.

remediation.command: Microsoft recommends namespaces as the logical isolation boundary for workloads and resources in shared clusters, combined with governance within each namespace such as quotas and network policies. Where stronger tenant isolation is required, Microsoft recommends separate clusters rather than relying on namespaces alone. 1. Create separate namespaces for each team, application, or environment that requires its own administrative scope. 2. Use managed namespaces when centralized configuration of access, quotas, network policies, labels, and annotations is appropriate. 3. Move user workloads out of the default namespace and into the appropriate namespace. 4. Rebind access using Role and RoleBinding objects in the required namespace, or Azure RBAC assignments limited to the required namespace where applicable. 5.

title: Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers
description: Apply securityContext settings to pods and containers so workload runtime behavior is explicitly constrained instead of relying on image defaults or permissive cluster admission. Microsoft’s current AKS pod security guidance identifies settings such as runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities, and seccompProfile. The benchmark marks this recommendation Manual.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.5.2 Apply Security Context to Your Pods and Containers

audit.command: Audit this control by reviewing workload manifests to confirm pod and container securityContext settings are explicitly defined and aligned to the AKS security baseline. In current AKS guidance, securityContext is the primary manifest mechanism for enforcing least privilege runtime behavior. AKS supports validating or enforcing these settings through Pod Security Admission and Deployment Safeguards. • Review pod specs for explicit securityContext settings at the pod and container level, including regular, init, and ephemeral containers.

remediation.command: Remediate by defining and enforcing a hardened pod and container security baseline for all application namespaces in AKS, then requiring workloads to declare the necessary securityContext fields in their manifests. Pod Security Admission is enabled by default and is applied with namespace labels. Microsoft’s pod security guidance recommends explicit settings such as execution without root access, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, limited capabilities, and seccompProfile. AKS Automatic already uses Deployment Safeguards with the Baseline Pod Security Standard in Enforce mode at create or update time. • Apply PSA restricted labels to general application namespaces that can meet the Restricted Pod Security Standard, using warn and audit first where rollout needs to be staged.

title: The default namespace should not be used
description: Avoid placing application workloads in the default namespace, and instead deploy them into dedicated namespaces that reflect the intended team, application, or environment boundary. Namespaces are the built in way to logically divide cluster resources and limit access, while the default namespace exists mainly so a cluster can be used immediately without first creating a new namespace. Requires kubectl read access; fails when the default namespace holds objects other than the kubernetes Service, kube-root-ca.crt ConfigMap and default ServiceAccount.
reference: CIS Azure Kubernetes Service Automatic (AKS Automatic) Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.5.3 The default namespace should not be used

audit.command:
out=$(kubectl get pods,services,configmaps,secrets,serviceaccounts,deployments,statefulsets,daemonsets,jobs,cronjobs,ingresses,roles,rolebindings -n default -o name) || exit 1
bad=$(printf '%s\n' "$out" | grep -v '^$' | sed 's#^\([a-z]*\)\.[^/]*/#\1/#' | grep -Evx 'service/kubernetes|configmap/kube-root-ca\.crt|serviceaccount/default')
if [ -z "$bad" ]; then echo compliant; else printf '%s\n' "$bad" | head -n 25; fi

remediation.command: Create dedicated namespaces for teams, applications, and environments, then require all new resources to be deployed into those namespaces instead of default. Namespaces are the logical boundary for workload administration, so remediation should include recreating existing resources in dedicated namespaces or AKS managed namespaces where used, applying RBAC and other controls within the required namespace, and reserving access throughout the cluster for true platform administrators only. Because the namespace field cannot be changed for most existing Kubernetes objects, recreate the resources in the destination namespace, validate the application, and then remove the original resources from default. Assign the Azure built in policy with Audit first, then use Deny after application resources have been migrated and approved exceptions have been addressed.
